stops.name: Emerald Bay
stops.teaser: The famous blue bay with a tiny island in it.
stops.map: Emerald Bay State Park, Highway 89, South Lake Tahoe, CA
stops.clue: Drive Highway 89 along the lake's southwest shore to the big overlook above a deep blue bay. A single tiny island sits in the middle, and a stone mansion hides on the shore below.
stops.safety: Highway 89 is narrow and winding, and the overlook parking fills up. Park only in marked spots, watch for people crossing the road, and keep behind the barriers at the overlook. The trail down to Vikingsholm is steep, so follow the signs and bring water. The lake is cold all year.
stops.field: Field notes pending: nobody has walked this stop for the app yet.

story: Emerald Bay is a glacier-carved inlet, about 1.7 miles long. It is part of a 1,533-acre California state park established in 1953. In 1969 it was named a National Natural Landmark.

Down at the shore is Vikingsholm, a 38-room Scandinavian-style mansion built in the summer of 1929 by Lora Josephine Knight. She bought 240 acres in the bay for $250,000. The architect was Lennart Palme, a relative by marriage.

Knight also built a small tea house on Fannette Island. The island has had several names. The first to stick, Coquette, was thought up by vacationers in 1866, and the current name is believed to be a misreading of it.
stops.fact: In 1994 the bay's water was added to the park, making it one of the first underwater parks of its kind in California.
stops.disputed: Sources disagree on where the name Fannette comes from. The common theory is that it is a mix-up of the earlier name Coquette, but that is a belief, not a proven fact.

claims.t: Emerald Bay has the only island in Lake Tahoe.
claims.why: Fannette Island is the only island in Lake Tahoe, according to Wikipedia.
It was built in the summer of 1929 by Lora Josephine Knight.

stops.name: Cave Rock
stops.teaser: A sacred rock with a highway tunnel drilled through it.
stops.map: Cave Rock Lake Tahoe Nevada State Park, US-50, NV
stops.clue: Drive to the Nevada side of the lake on Highway 50 and find the big volcanic rock that the road goes through, near the boat launch.
stops.safety: Park only at the boat launch lot and keep off Highway 50, which has tunnels and narrow shoulders. Do not climb the rock. Climbing is banned, and the Washoe consider it sacred.

story: Cave Rock is sacred to the Washoe people. Wikipedia says tribal leaders were not consulted about the highway tunnels. The old Washoe trail and Johnson's Cut-Off Road went over the rock, while the Lake Tahoe Wagon Road and the Lincoln Highway went around it.

The first tunnel opened in 1931 and carries traffic through the rock. Construction of the second tunnel began in 1957. The westbound tunnel is 153 feet long and the eastbound one is 410 feet. The tunnels sit at about 6,360 feet above sea level, about 80 feet above the lake.

In 1967 the Nevada Legislature gave the boat launch and parking area to the state park system. The U.S. Forest Service banned rock climbing equipment on February 9, 1997, and the state says climbing has been prohibited under all circumstances since September 2, 2003.
stops.fact: The second tunnel cost just over $450,000.
stops.disputed: Sources differ on the climbing ban: the state park history says September 2, 2003, and Wikipedia mentions a 2007 federal ruling. Both agree that climbing is not allowed.

claims.why: Wikipedia: the Washoe Tribe considers Cave Rock sacred.

stops.name: Kings Beach
stops.teaser: A long sandy beach on the north shore, named for a postmaster.
stops.map: Kings Beach State Recreation Area, Kings Beach, CA
stops.clue: Go to the north shore, in California, near the Nevada line. A wide sandy beach with a view straight across the lake is right next to the main road.
stops.safety: The beach is next to Highway 28, so cross only at marked crossings and watch for cars and bikes. The water is cold. Keep an eye on younger kids near the water.
stops.field: Field notes pending: nobody has walked this stop for the app yet.

story: The town is named after its first postmaster, Joe King. It sits on the north shore at about 6,444 feet.
The post office was built in 1937. The 2020 census counted 3,563 residents.
Kings Beach is also a place where wildlife and people share space. In 2009 and 2010, beavers were removed from nearby Griff Creek, and local schoolchildren protested.
stops.fact: Lake Tahoe is about 22 miles long, up to 12 miles wide, and 1,645 feet deep at its deepest.
stops.disputed: Our sources do not give an exact founding date for Kings Beach, so we do not claim one.

claims.t: Kings Beach is named after its first postmaster.
claims.why: Wikipedia says it is named after its first postmaster, Joe King.

claims.t: Lake Tahoe is more than 3,000 feet deep.
claims.why: The maximum depth is 1,645 feet, still the second deepest lake in the U.S.

stops.name: Camp Richardson
stops.teaser: A lakeside resort that has been welcoming visitors for a century.
stops.map: Camp Richardson Resort, Emerald Bay Rd, South Lake Tahoe, CA
stops.clue: On the south shore, a few miles west of the town of South Lake Tahoe, find a long beach with a marina, cabins and a lodge. Snowy peaks rise across the water.
stops.safety: Highway 89 runs beside the resort, so cross at marked spots and watch for bikes on the shared path. The water is cold. Stay on paths and out of private cabin areas.
stops.field: Field notes pending: nobody has walked this stop for the app yet.

q.hint: Camp Richardson is on the lake's south shore. Use your phone's compass.
q.verify: Camp Richardson is on the south shore, so facing the lake means facing north. Confirm with a compass on site.

story: The resort is named after Captain Alonzo L. Richardson, who started a stage service from Placerville to South Lake Tahoe in 1921. He was also the first postmaster in the area.
An 1891 U.S. Geological Survey map shows the site as Yanks. The Camp Richardson post office ran from 1927 to 1973, with a closure in 1964 and 1965.
Today the resort has a marina, cabins, hotel rooms and a bar and grill, at about 6,250 feet above sea level.
stops.fact: The Camp Richardson post office operated for almost half a century, from 1927 to 1973.
stops.disputed: Accounts differ on who gets credit for the resort's start. Richardson leased the land in 1921, but a later figure, Ray Kinsley, helped keep the area from being over-commercialized.

claims.why: Wikipedia says the camp was established in 1921 by Captain Alonzo Richardson.

claims.t: The site was always called Camp Richardson.
claims.why: An 1891 USGS map labels it Yanks.

mission: Visit four of Lake Tahoe's best-known spots, one on each shore. At each one, check in to earn its badge, unlock its story, and collect a Time Card. Do them in any order. Everything stays on this phone.
afterDone: All four badges earned. You have done the big four. Ready for the Hidden Gems?
safetyNote: • These stops are spread around the lake, so plan the drive. Highway 89 and Highway 28 are busy and winding, so park in marked spots and cross at crosswalks. The lake is cold all year and the area is high, so bring water and sun protection.
